§ 1.4:3 Judgment at or after trial
See Alberta Rules of Court, Alta. Reg. 124/2010, r. 1.4.
1. Re-opening Trial
The plaintiff applies by Notice of Motion to reopen the trial [(1993), 12 Alta. L.R. 298] of the within action for the purpose of adducing further evidence—evidence of the forgery of trial Ex. 171…
The law in this application is well settled and agreed to by counsel. There are 3 factors to be considered in deciding this application:
1. The fundamental consideration is that a miscarriage of justice does not occur and therefore the discretion is unfettered. In this regard, it is important to keep in mind that regard must be had to the interests of the defendant as well as those of the plaintiff.
2. Once reasons have been given, the successful party is not to be deprived of it without very solid grounds.
3. The greatest care must be exercised to avoid abuse of the court's process.
Factor 2 further requires that the new evidence to be adduced be incontrovertible. Overseas Investments (1986) Ltd. v. Cornwall Developments Ltd. (1995), 36 Alta. L.R. (3d) 53 (Q.B.), at 54-55, per Foster J.
In Kay v. Wirstiuk (1977), 8 A.R. 405 (Q.B.), Steer J. had before him an “application to re-open a trial to hear new evidence after reasons for judgment were given but before entry of the judgment roll”. At p. 412, His Lordship summarized the applicable law:
My conclusion is that the following are the three general factors that must be weighed in this kind of application:
(1) The fundamental consideration is that a miscarriage of justice does not occur and therefore the discretion [is] unfettered. In this regard it is important to keep in mind that regard must be had to the interests of the defendant as well as those of the plaintiff.
(2) Once reasons have been given, the successful party is not to be deprived of it without very solid grounds.
(3) The greatest care must be exercised to avoid abuse of the Court's process.
The particular matters to be considered in exercising the discretion and in determining whether the applicant's grounds are solid are:
(a) Was the issue with respect to which the new evidence is sought to be adduced recognized and dealt with at the trial, or is counsel surprised and unable therefore to properly deal with the question by evidence?
(b) Is the evidence sought to be adduced incontrovertible in the sense that it is a fact that exists and evidence cannot be called to negative its existence? If so, and had it been adduced at trial, might it probably have altered the decision on that issue and the final result, having regard to the other evidence adduced at the trial?
In Ernst & Young Inc. v. Central Guaranty Trust Co. (1998), 221 A.R. 173 (Q.B.); [affirming on reconsideration (1998) 227 A.R. 300 (Q.B.)], Clarke J. referred to the above excerpt from Kay v. Wirstiuk (1977), 8 A.R. 405 (Q.B.), with approval. Clarke J. went on to discuss the standard to be applied for reconsideration in complex cases. At p. 174, Clarke J. said:
Very high standards are set by the court where a party seeks to tender new evidence after a trial and a decision has been given or after an order has been entered. In complex litigation where there are ongoing interlocutory matters, that standard for entertaining a reconsideration of the matter, in my view, is too high. Recognizing the merit in promoting some finality and in discouraging counsel from simply “trying again” the court nonetheless in this type of litigation should exercise greater flexibility in entertaining a reconsideration application. The mass of information and documentation in this type of litigation and the fact that the application is an interlocutory application both justify a less rigorous standard.
Kay v. Wirstiuk (1977), 8 A.R. 405 (Q.B.), was applied in both Luscar Ltd. v. Pembina Resources Ltd. (1992), 2 Alta. L.R. (3d) 157 (Q.B.), per Egbert J., and James J. Zelazo Professional Corp. v. Montgomery (1998), 229 A.R. 324, per Moreau J.
2. Judgments in Segments
… typically, a judgment will be given at one time, and will deal with all issues that are before it. However, an overall principle of law, including the law relating to judgments and orders, is that rules must advance fairness, not impede it. Therefore, if fairness requires that a judgment be delivered in segments, the court will do so.
Indeed, the general rule about judgments is frequently varied. The most frequent exception to the rule applies in relation to that part of the judgment dealing with costs. Our Court of Appeal has indicated that costs can virtually always be separated from the substantive decision, and that no harm comes from that: [Husky Oil Operations v. Forest Oil Corp. (1991), 79 Alta. L.R. (2d) 134 (C.A.)].
Another common situation arises where a judge makes a decision about a matter of principle that is in dispute, and then sends the case to a referee to decide one practical aspect of the dispute. The judge will then incorporate the referee's decision into the overall judgment.
Other examples can be taken from family law. In [Stephenson v. Stephenson (1968), 67 W.W.R. 222 (B.C. C.A.)], the British Columbia Court of Appeal indicated that a judgment that dealt with both the dissolution of a marriage and with awarding damages for a matrimonial fault was severable. If a judgment can be severed, it can also be divided. 155569 Canada Ltd. v. 248524 Alberta Ltd. (1995), 37 Alta. L.R. (3d) 51 (Q.B.), at 56, per Veit J.
3. When Is a Court Functus?
The issue of whether judgments should be given at one time also raises a related issue: Does a judge become functus once she has issued a portion of a judgment?
We normally think of the rule of functus in this way: once a judge has pronounced judgment, that judge has lost jurisdiction. The rule advances the policy objective of bringing litigation to finality. That objective is so powerful that some judges would go so far as to prevent the re-opening of a judgment even where fraud has been proved: [Flower v. Lloyd (1879), 10 Ch. D. 327 (C.A.)].
Nonetheless, we are aware that there are exceptions to the rule of functus. The English Court of Appeal has indicated that a judge who is delivering a judgment orally, and is given information which reveals a statement he has just made is incorrect, is not necessarily functus: [Cheeseman v. Bowaters United Kingdom Paper Mill Ltd., [1971] 3 All E.R. 513 (C.A.)].
However, the main exception to the rule of functus is the ability of a judge who has rendered judgment to “work out” the terms of the judgment.
The English Court of Appeal also reminds us that there is no set list of exceptions to the rule of functus. Law must always be free to do justice. In [Thynne v. Thynne, [1955] 3 All E.R. 129 (C.A.)], we find the following comments from Morris L.J.:
It would, I think, be undesirable to limit the scope of these powers [to make amendments in the terms of its orders and judgments] as a result of any words which describe them. I respectfully agree with what was indicated by Evershed L.J., in Meier v. Meier when he said: ‘I prefer not to attempt a definition of the extent of the court's inherent jurisdiction to vary, modify or extend its own orders if, in its view, the purposes of justice require that it should do so.’
I adopt the comments, and citation, of Morris L.J. as my own. 155569 Canada Ltd. v. 248524 Alberta Ltd. (1995), 37 Alta. L.R. (3d) 51 (Q.B.), at 56-57, per Veit J.
In Pro-Express Ltd. v. Thew (1996), 185 A.R. 285 (Q.B.), Russell J. (as she then was) dealt with “an application for leave to argue or re-argue a matter arising from a trial in which judgment has been granted, but not entered”. In determining that she had jurisdiction to do so, her Ladyship said at p. 286:
Because judgment has not been entered, I am not “functus”: Stevenson v. Dandy, [1918] 3 W.W.R. 662 (Alta. C.A.). Even at this stage, a trial judge has discretion to permit further evidence to be adduced or further argument, to prevent a miscarriage of justice. That discretion must be sparingly exercised to prevent abuses of the court's process. It should not be exercised unless it might, on the balance of probabilities, affect the result: Vance v. Vance, [1982] 2 W.W.R. 472 (B.C. S.C.).
In Condominium Plan No. 7510189 v. Jones (1997), 48 Alta. L.R. (3d) 281 (C.A.), the court said at p. 289:
“The general rule is clear that once an order is passed and entered or otherwise perfected in accordance with the practice of the Court, the Court which passed the order is functus officio and cannot set aside or alter the order however wrong it may appear to be. That can only be done on appeal”: Plyaratana Unnanse v. Wahareke Sonuttara Unnanse, [1950] 2 W.W.R. 796 at 800 (P.C.); see also Paper Machinery Ltd. v. J.O. Ross Engineering Corp., [1934] 2 D.L.R. 239 (S.C.C.); Singh (Banns) v. Bank of Montreal (1979), [1980] 3 W.W.R. 403 (B.C. C.A.). The two exceptions to this rule are: (1) where there has been a slip in drawing up the judgment; and (2) where the judgment as entered does not truly express the intention of the Court: Paper Machinery Ltd. v. J.O. Ross Engineering Corp., (supra), at 240; Guaranty Trust Co. of Canada v. Country Plaza Investors Ltd. (1983), 47 A.R. 184 (Master).
In Iverson v. Westfair Foods Ltd. (1998), 67 Alta. L.R. (3d) 148 (C.A.); [leave to appeal refused (1999) 244 A.R. 400n (S.C.C.)], O'Leary J.A., speaking for the majority, said, at p. 167:
The 1990 Order was a final order with respect to the remedy directed. In our view, the Chambers judge was functus officio in that respect and had no jurisdiction to direct in the 1995 Order that the Class A shareholders sell their shares to Westfair. The general rule is that a final judgment or order cannot be set aside or varied by the judge who made it, or by a judge of the same court, after it has been drawn up and entered. There are two exceptions: (i) where there has been a slip in drawing up the judgment or order, and (ii) where there has been an error in expressing the manifest intention of the court… It follows that a judge has no jurisdiction to interpret his own order after it has been drawn up and entered.
In Wooldridge v. Wooldridge (1999), 250 A.R. 168 (C.A.), the Court of Appeal confirmed that if an order is not yet entered, then the granting court is not functus. At p. 169, the court said:
The respondent argues that according to rule 322 of the Rules of Court our judgment must take effect from the day it is pronounced “unless otherwise directed.” Since our Judgment is silent in this regard, he implies that this court is now “functus”. We do not agree. Because the Order of this court has not yet been filed, we reject the suggestion that this court is “functus”.
In 369413 Alberta Ltd. v. Pocklington (2000), 79 Alta. L.R. (3d) 222 (Q.B.), Mason, J. said at pp. 228-9:
… I am satisfied that the case law establishes that I am not functus officio either after granting an order or issuing reasons for judgment unless and until the order or judgment is signed and entered. That conclusion is based on the ratio of the case of Harrison's Share under a Settlement, Re, [1955] 1 All E. R. 185 (Eng. C.A.). Jenkins L.J., who wrote for the Court, reviewed a number of English authorities with a view to clarifying the law on when a judge is functus officio. The following quotation addresses the issue on point:
Our answer to this is that, although the judgment dates from the day of its pronouncement, it is not perfected until drawn up, passed and entered, and anyone who acts on it beforehand must take such risk as there is that it will not be drawn in the form in which it was heard to be pronounced.
We think that an order pronounced by the judge can always be withdrawn, or altered or modified, by him until it is drawn up, passed and entered. In the meantime it is provisionally effective, and can be treated as a subsisting order in cases where the justice of the case requires it, and the right of withdrawal would not be thereby prevented or prejudiced. For example, the granting of an injunction, though open to review, would generally operate immediately, i.e., as soon as the relevant words are spoken. But an order which could only be treated as operative at the expense of making it, in effect, irrevocable, e.g., an order for payment of money, cannot be treated as operative until it has been passed and entered.
The Court then considered a number of authorities and assessed submissions as to the immediacy and efficacy of the appeal process to resolve the issue. Jenkins L.J., speaking for the Court, stated that no judge is functus until the order or judgment is drawn, passed and entered. A judge may on the motion of one of the parties or on his/her own motion determine there is a proper matter to be addressed before the order or judgment is finalized. Jenkins L.J., at 192, made these two observations:
It is important to remember that, in the ordinary way, the recall of an unperfected order results in a rehearing at which all parties can present such further arguments as they may be advised having regard to the matter, whatever it may be, which is sought to cast doubt on the correctness of the order as already pronounced. …
When a judge has pronounced judgment he retains control over the case until the order giving effect to his judgment is formally completed. This control must be used in accordance with his discretion exercised judicially and not capriciously.
… This statement of the law has been recognized in Alberta.
4. Purpose of Stay of Execution
In my view, the purpose of a stay of execution is to prevent an appeal from being nugatory. What that means is that if an appeal succeeds, the successful appellant should not find that he has already permanently lost all the benefits which the appeal is supposed to give him, so that the appeal has become academic. Alberta (Minister of Consumer & Corporate Affairs) v. Bennett (1992), 131 A.R. 184 (C.A.), at 185, per Côté J.A.
5. Principles to Be Applied in Application for Stay
This question does not frequently come before our courts because the common practice for many years, in cases where the financial responsibility of the defendant is in no doubt, has been for the successful plaintiff to hold proceedings under his judgment in abeyance pending determination of the appeal. This reflects proper consideration of the fact that the issue between the parties is still in litigation. It also undoubtedly reflects some appreciation for the change in applicable conditions which have occurred since the rule was first applied and a standard of procedure laid down …
It is not the practice of the court to deprive a successful party of the fruits of the litigation until an appeal is disposed of except under special circumstances. The fact that the respondent will be unable to repay the amount levied by execution if the appeal is successful is a special circumstance which warrants an order for a stay … There must, however, be evidence which shows that if the judgment is paid there is no reasonable probability of getting the money repaid in case the appeal is successful …[quoting Athabaska Airways Ltd. v. Sask. Govt. Airways (1958), 24 W.W.R. 379 at 380 (Sask. C.A.)].
Lord Cotton, in Wilson v. Church (No. 2) (1879), 12 Ch D 454, at 458 … in stating:
I will state my opinion that when a party is appealing, exercising his undoubted right of appeal, this Court ought to see that the appeal, if successful, is not nugatory; …
effectively expressed one phase, or part of the consideration required, in applying the rule.
These decisions establish that the rule is designed to enable the court to protect either litigant as may be required under the particular circumstances of the case, pending determination of the appeal. For instance, a successful plaintiff should not be prejudiced through delay in enforcing his judgment if, in the interval, the defendant might so change his position or assets as to create the prejudice; a defendant should not be subjected to the obligation of immediate payment if, assuming success in the appeal, repayment is not reasonably certain and this without undue delay. Leskovar v. Saskatchewan Government Insurance Office (1965), 51 W.W.R. 46 (Sask. C.A.), at 47-48, per Maguire J.A.
And Purvis J. said:
Rule 346(2) provides that the court may stay execution at any time after judgment. The effect of the stay is the same whether it is granted at the time judgment is given or at a later date. First City Trust Co. v. S & S Homes (Edmonton) Ltd. (1983), 26 Alta. L.R. (2d) 226 at 227 (Q.B.).
Rule 346(2) then read as follows:
(2) The court may, at or after the time judgment is given, stay execution or may remove or extend any stay already granted.
Côté J.A., in Jager Industries Inc. v. Leduc (County) No. 25 (1997), 55 Alta. L.R. (3d) 77 (C.A.), specifically addressed stays of money judgments. A large monetary award was made against Jager who then sought a stay of the award. The evidence showed that both parties could pay or repay the sum involved. At pp. 79-80, his Lordship said:
Jager's counsel suggest that the applicable test is like that for interlocutory injunctions, featuring irreparable harm and balance of convenience. (Serious question to try is conceded here for this motion only.)
However, I have grave doubts that that is the proper test where what is to be stayed is a money injunction…
It is not necessary to settle those mysteries here. The traditional test in money cases makes the applicant (appellant) prove a special need for a stay, usually by showing that if the judgment were paid, the respondent would likely have trouble repaying it …
Traditionally, the fact that the appellant would have trouble paying the judgment is not ground for a stay …A fortiori when he could pay, but it would deprive him of the benefits of having the money.
. . . . .
This case illustrates the soundness of the traditional approach in Alberta. If both parties are good for this sum and will remain so, there should be no stay of a money judgment barring some unusual circumstances.
In Stochinsky v. Chetner (2002), 316 A.R. 244 (Q.B.), Mason J., at p. 246, provided the following summary of the test for a stay of execution:
I conclude from these authorities that the tripartite test used in determining interlocutory injunctive relief is also the test to be applied for stay applications, i.e., (1) a prima facie or serious issue to be tried, (2) demonstrable irreparable harm, and (3) the balance of convenience favouring the stay; Metropolitan Stores (MTS) Ltd. v. Manitoba Food and Commercial Workers, Local 832 and Labour Board (Man.), [1987] 1 S.C.R. 110, 73 N.R. 341, 46 Man. R. (2d) 241, 38 D.L.R. (4th) 321. The test is to be applied to both non-monetary as well as monetary judgments, except that in the case of monetary judgments, the applicant for the stay must overcome the presumption that money judgments are entitled to be enforced without more. This presumption brings into play at least the following considerations:
(a) The amount of the money judgment, having regard to the respective positions of the parties;
(b) The ability of the party against whom the stay is sought to repay the judgment if the applicant is successful on appeal;
(c) Evidence of any other special need for a stay.
6. Abuse of Process
In Feuerhelm v. Alberta (Justice and Attorney General), 2017 ABQB 709, 2017 CarswellAlta 2506, Justice Eamon discussed the concept of “abuse of process”:
79 This Court has inherent jurisdiction to prevent misuse of its procedure in a way that would be manifestly unfair to a litigant or would bring the administration of justice into disrepute. In Toronto (City) v CUPE, 2003 SCC 63, [2003] 3 SCR 77 the Court stated:
35 Judges have an inherent and residual discretion to prevent an abuse of the court's process. This concept of abuse of process was described at common law as proceedings “unfair to the point that they are contrary to the interest of justice” (R. v. Power, [1994] 1 S.C.R. 601, at p. 616), and as “oppressive treatment” (R. v. Conway, [1989] 1 S.C.R. 1659, at p. 1667). McLachlin J. (as she then was) expressed it this way in R. v. Scott, [1990] 3 S.C.R. 979, at p. 1007:
… abuse of process may be established where: (1) the proceedings are oppressive or vexatious; and, (2) violate the fundamental principles of justice underlying the community's sense of fair play and decency. The concepts of oppressiveness and vexatiousness underline the interest of the accused in a fair trial. But the doctrine evokes as well the public interest in a fair and just trial process and the proper administration of justice.
36 The doctrine of abuse of process is used in a variety of legal contexts. The unfair or oppressive treatment of an accused may disentitle the Crown to carry on with the prosecution of a charge: Conway, supra, at p. 1667. In Blencoe v. British Columbia (Human Rights Commission), [2000] 2 S.C.R. 307, 2000 SCC 44, this Court held that unreasonable delay causing serious prejudice could amount to an abuse of process. When the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms applies, the common law doctrine of abuse of process is subsumed into the principles of the Charter such that there is often overlap between abuse of process and constitutional remedies (R. v. O'Connor, [1995] 4 S.C.R. 411). The doctrine nonetheless continues to have application as a non-Charter remedy: United States of America v. Shulman, [2001] 1 S.C.R. 616, 2001 SCC 21, at para. 33.
37 In the context that interests us here, the doctrine of abuse of process engages “the inherent power of the court to prevent the misuse of its procedure, in a way that would … bring the administration of justice into disrepute” (Canam Enterprises Inc. v. Coles (2000), 51 O.R. (3d) 481 (C.A.), at para. 55, per Goudge J.A., dissenting (approved [2002] 3 S.C.R. 307, 2002 SCC 63)). Goudge J.A. expanded on that concept in the following terms at paras. 55-56:
The doctrine of abuse of process engages the inherent power of the court to prevent the misuse of its procedure, in a way that would be manifestly unfair to a party to the litigation before it or would in some other way bring the administration of justice into disrepute. It is a flexible doctrine unencumbered by the specific requirements of concepts such as issue estoppel. See House of Spring Gardens Ltd. v. Waite, [1990] 3 W.L.R. 347 at p. 358, [1990] 2 All E.R. 990 (C.A.).
…
[Underlining in passage quoted]
80 The doctrine of abuse of process concentrates on the integrity and fairness of the adjudicative process (CUPE at para 51; Behn v Moulton Contracting Ltd., 2013 SCC 26, [2013] 2 SCR 227, at para 41). The doctrine of abuse of process is not limited to acts giving rise to an unfair hearing; there may be cases of abuse of process for other than evidentiary reasons (Blencoe at para 115). The latter type of case arises where there is where unfairness or vexatiousness of such a degree that it contravenes fundamental notions of justice and thus undermines the integrity of the judicial process (Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration) v Tobiass, [1997] 3 SCR 391 at para 89).
81 The remedy of a stay is prospective and intended to protect the judicial process. Thus a stay may be granted where the abuse has resulted in destruction of vital evidence required for a fair trial or other forms of misconduct that go to trial fairness (R v Gangl, 2011 ABCA 357 at paras 8–10). A stay of proceedings usually will only be appropriate when two criteria are met: (1) the prejudice to the accused's right to a fair trial or the integrity of the justice system caused by the abuse in question will be manifested, perpetuated or aggravated through the conduct of the trial, or by its outcome; and (2) no other remedy is reasonably capable of removing that prejudice (O'Connor at para 75; Tobias at para 89–91). Where there is still uncertainty, the court is required to balance the interests in favour of granting a stay, such as denouncing misconduct and preserving the integrity of the justice system, against the interest that society has in having a final decision on the merits (R v Gambilla (appeal by Mamouni), 2017 ABCA 347 at paras 37–39). This test has been applied in civil proceedings brought by the state (Tobiass at para 89–91).
7. Modified Test in Custody Disputes
In B. (C.) v. C. (P.) (2003), 346 A.R. 121 (C.A.), Russell J.A. noted that the triparte test is modified when the Court is dealing with the custody of a child. At pp. 122-123:
The tripartite test established in RJR-MacDonald Inc. et Imperial Tobacco Ltd. v. Canada (Procureur général), [1994] 1 S.C.R. 311, 164 N.R. 1, 60 Q.A.C. 241, is the applicable test when considering whether a stay should be granted. There are three questions to be considered. First, is there is a serious question to be argued on appeal that is neither vexatious nor frivolous. In the circumstances of a custody or access order, the threshold for this part of the test is not elevated to require a demonstration of the merits of the case: G.R. v. C.M., [2003] A.R. Uned. 418, 2003 ABCA 268 (C.A.); Fielding v. Steele (1995), 174 A.R. 296, 102 W.A.C. 296 (C.A.); and Slezak v. Slezak (1993), 149 A.R. 51, 63 W.A.C. 51 (C.A.). The second and third parts of the test, to be considered together, are whether the applicant would suffer irreparable harm if the stay is refused and, on a balance of convenience, who would suffer greater inconvenience?
In all matters dealing with the custody of a child, the overriding principle is the best interests of the child: Gordon v. Goertz, [1996] 2 S.C.R. 27, 196 N.R. 321, 141 Sask. R. 241, 114 W.A.C. 241, ¶ 28; Fielding, supra, at para. 10. Consequently, in determining whether a stay should be granted pending the appeal of a custody or access order, some courts have explicitly modified the tripartite test in the context of custody and access orders: See: Lefebvre v. Lefebvre (2002), 167 O.A.C. 85 (C.A.); T.G. v. Mi'kmaw Family and Children's Services (2003), 211 N.S.R. (2d) 218, 62 A.P.R. 218 (C.A.). “[T]his Court has considered stays of custody Orders on the ground that if special circumstances exist that could be harmful to a child if the Order were acted upon before the appeal was heard, a stay would be granted …”: Fulton Insurance Agencies Ltd. v. Purdy (1991), 100 N.S.R. (2d) 341, 272 A.P.R. 341 (C.A.). Although not previously explicitly articulated, it is clear that this Court has also applied a modified tripartite test: See G.R. v. C.M., supra; Slezak, supra at para. 7; Fielding, supra at para. 10. For the purpose of providing greater certainty, it should be underscored that in considering an application for a stay in a matter of custody or access, the second and third branch of the tripartite test must be modified to reflect the paramount importance of the best interests of the child. Those interests mandate a consideration of whether the child will suffer irreparable harm from the denial of a stay, and it is those interests that will ultimately determine the balance of convenience. Any harm to the applicants from the denial of a stay is thus subordinate to the best interests of the child.
8. Undertaking Not Required
In Masse v. Alberta Racing Commission (1995), 177 A.R. 79 (Q.B.), Madam Justice Veit had before her an application for a stay of sanctions imposed upon the applicant by the Alberta Racing Commission. At issue was whether the applicant had to supply an undertaking in damages in support of the application. At p. 80, her Ladyship said:
Although the applicant for a stay must meet many of the standards required of a litigant applying for an interlocutory injunction, filing an undertaking in damages is not required.
The difference between an application for a stay and an application for an interlocutory injunction is that in the case of a stay, the party opposite already has the benefit of a decision or judgment. The only thing that might be required, in some circumstances, of an applicant for a stay is security of costs… There is no need for an undertaking in damages when a party applies for a stay. The other side already has the benefit of a decision or judgment; the judgment awards them damages or the decision gives them the relief they originally sought.
As opposed to that situation, when asking for an interlocutory injunction, a person who does not yet have judicially awarded rights asks the court to intervene in the business of another litigant. It is obviously appropriate, in such circumstances, for the person making the request to give an undertaking to indemnify the party opposite should the court not uphold the right they are seeking to assert.
Note the comments of Côté J.A. in Jager Industries Inc. v. Leduc (County) No. 25 (1997), 55 Alta. L.R. (3d) 77 (C.A.), under “Principles To Be Applied in Application for Stay”.

1.5. Rule contravention, non-compliance and irregularities
(1) If a person contravenes or does not comply with any procedural requirement, or if there is an irregularity in a commencement document, pleading, document, affidavit or prescribed form, a party may apply to the Court
(a) to cure the contravention, non-compliance or irregularity, or
(b) to set aside an act, application, proceeding or other thing because of prejudice to that party arising from the contravention, non-compliance or irregularity.
(2) An application under this rule must be filed within a reasonable time after the applicant becomes aware of the contravention, non-compliance or irregularity.
(3) An application under this rule may not be filed by a party who alleges prejudice as a result of the contravention, non-compliance or irregularity if that party has taken a further step in the action knowing of the prejudice.
(4) The Court must not cure any contravention, non-compliance or irregularity unless
(a) to do so will cause no irreparable harm to any party,
(b) in doing so the Court imposes terms or conditions that will
(i) eliminate or ameliorate any reparable harm, or
(ii) prevent the recurrence of the contravention, non-compliance or irregularity,
(c) in doing so the Court imposes a suitable sanction, if any, for the contravention, non-compliance or irregularity, and
(d) it is in the overall interests of justice to cure the contravention, non-compliance or irregularity.
(5) The Court must not cure any contravention, non-compliance or irregularity if to do so would have the effect of extending a time period that the Court is prohibited from extending.
(6) If an order is made under this rule, the Court may also impose a penalty under rule 10.49.

§ 1.5:1 Rule 1.5

1. General
In Feeney v. Alberta, 2021 ABCA 398, 2021 CarswellAlta 308, Justice Watson said, at paragraphs 10-11:
[10] … Unwarranted and unjust exemptions from rules of procedure are as undesirable as unreasonable and unjust enforcements of such rules. This general principle also applies to applications which unrepresented parties may launch whether or not they are clearly expressed to be associated with any specific rule or requirement. As stated in Carbone v Whidden, 2015 ABCA 177 at para 14, [2015] AJ No 557 (QL):
14 Some of the grounds argued (in writing and orally) for the applicant's unusual request are that self-represented parties should have special rights not allowed to parties with counsel. A great mass of authority contrary to that proposition could be cited. And from a policy point of view, such a rule would be most unfair.
[11] While the applicant's position as to condonation does not go so far as in Carbone, it is useful to reinforce the proposition that courts are to administer equal justice under law, and while that may involve lenience to error on occasion, justice must also remain neutral. …
In Kwadrans v. Kwadrans, 2023 ABCA 203, 2023 CarswellAlta 1751, the Court said, at paragraph 35:
…The general rule 1.5 should not be invoked if there is a specific rule that addresses the issue in question, here being rule 3.2(6): see Makar v. Luedey, 2013 ABQB 189 at para 16; see also Ruth Sullivan, The Construction of Statutes, 7th ed (LexisNexis Canada Inc, 2022) at § 11.05. …
2. Time Requirements of the Rule
In Hansraj v. Ao, 2004 ABCA 223, 2004 CarswellAlta 849, 354 A.R. 91, 34 Alta. L.R. (4th) 199, Côté J.A. set out the time requirements for bringing a successful application under the Rule. At p. 207, his Lordship said:
The appellants cite R. 559, which sets two time limits for a motion “to set aside any process or proceedings for irregularity”. Such a motion must be brought
(a) within a reasonable time, and
(b) before “the party applying has taken a fresh step after knowledge of the irregularity”.
When the party moving learned of the defect is critical to both (a) and (b). The party would delay unreasonably if he did not move when he first learned the facts. …
Even though what I call branch (b) of R. 559 does not speak expressly of what the party moving should have known, I would read that into the Rule. And if I am wrong there, to move long after one should have learned of the flaw with reasonable care, is to move outside a reasonable time.
3. Schedules must be “flexible”
In Brinton v. Coish, 2017 ABCA 334, 2017 CarswellAlta 1822, the Court said:
5 Litigation schedules and orders setting time limits are designed to fulfil the overall objective of R. 1.2 in having litigation “fairly and justly resolved … in a timely and cost effective way”. Plans and schedules must always be flexible enough to adapt to changed circumstances, new information, the unavailability of counsel and witnesses, and other circumstances that might arise. That is so whether the procedures are agreed to by counsel, or are contained in a consent or other order. Deadlines and other agreed procedures must not be ignored, but they must not be allowed to overcome the ultimate objective of deciding litigation on the merits. Depriving the trier of fact of relevant evidence is counterproductive.
6 The Rules of Court enable that sort of flexibility. Rule 1.5(4) specifically provides that non-compliance can be cured as long as there is no irreparable harm to either party, and curing the non-compliance would not be contrary to the interests of justice. …
4. “Lateness”—Important comment regarding unintended consequences
In Sobeys West Inc. v. Edmonton (City), 2015 ABCA 32, 2015 CarswellAlta 93, Justice Slatter said, at paragraphs 18-19:
18 Failure to meet the deadlines in R. 14.40(2) and R. 14.41 has various consequences. Rule 14.90(1)(a)(i) contains a presumption that no costs are available for a late step. The Registry or the presiding judge may decline to set down a matter that has missed the deadline, depending on the number of matters scheduled that week and other considerations. Late filing by a respondent will not be allowed to prejudice an applicant: R. 1.5(4). Extreme cases of missed deadlines can result in appeals or applications being struck.
19 Litigants before the Court should, however, be aware that there is another meaning of “lateness” in this context. The Registry will deliver the application materials for any particular week to the presiding judge before some of these formal deadlines are reached. Documents filed after that date are “late”, in the sense that the rest of the material will already have been sent to the judge. While “last minute” filings will not be subject to the consequences mentioned in para. 18, lateness in filing may require an adjournment of the hearing into the future. Whether that is necessary depends on a number of factors, including the complexity of the application, the volume of material, the number of applications set down that week, and the other responsibilities of the presiding judge. Prudent counsel will file early, and certainly will not wait until the Monday after the weekend to file documents.
5. Irregularities seldom result in a proceeding being “void”
In Thompson v. Procrane Inc., 2016 ABCA 71, 2016 CarswellAlta 430, an Originating Application was deficient in respect of the time it set for the hearing of the application. Justice Slatter noted that R. 13.5(2) allowed the Court to abridge the time requirement, and that R. 1.5(1) allowed the Court to remedy an irregularity. His Lordship concluded, at paragraph 9:
… Contrary to the applicant's expectation, irregularities in procedure rarely if ever amount to a proceeding being “void”: Mazepa v Embree, 2014 ABCA 438, 14 Alta LR (6th) 83, 588 AR 288.
